title: Slab-built herb pot tray
subtitle: A rectangular air-dry clay tray for three small herb pots with a raised rim and drainage channel
excerpt: A herb pot tray is a rectangular slab-built dish in air-dry clay, sized to hold three small pots in a row on a windowsill. The raised rim keeps pots from sliding, and a shallow channel cut into the base guides water away from pot bases. No kiln is needed. Beginner makers who have rolled a slab before can complete this project in one sitting.
sourceNotes: Slab-building method derived from first principles. Functional tray proportions scaled to standard 9 cm herb pot diameter.

glossaryTerms.definition: A flat sheet of clay rolled to an even thickness, used as the building unit in slab construction
The stage at which clay holds its shape firmly but remains damp enough to join and trim
Fully air-dried and unfired; pale and lightweight, ready for sealing
The joining method: roughen both clay surfaces with a needle, apply clay slip, then press together firmly

content.text: A herb pot tray is a rectangular
slab

-built dish in air-dry clay, sized to hold three small herb pots in a row on a kitchen windowsill. The finished tray measures approximately 35 cm long by 12 cm wide, with 3 cm raised walls and a shallow drainage channel cut into the base. No kiln is needed. A beginner who has done basic slab rolling can complete this project in a single session.

materials.name: Clay slip (same clay body, thinned with water)
PVA glue diluted 50/50 with water (for sealing)

content.text: Preparation

Measure the three pots you plan to use. A standard small herb pot is about 9 cm across at the widest point of the base. The tray interior should be at least 11 cm wide so the pots fit with clearance. For three pots in a row, the interior length needs to be at least 33 cm. These instructions use a final interior size of 33 cm long by 10 cm wide. Adjust the dimensions to fit your specific pots. Roll all your slabs before beginning the joins, so the clay stiffens evenly.
Making the tray

Roll a slab 7 mm thick using guide strips of equal height on each side. Cut a rectangle 35 cm by 12 cm for the base. This is slightly larger than the interior to allow for the wall thickness. Place on a flat canvas or board.

Cut the drainage channel into the base slab now, before the walls go on. Mark a line 2 cm in from each long edge, running the full length of the base. Use the needle tool to score a shallow channel 3 mm wide and 3 mm deep between these marks, running down the centre of the tray. This central channel will guide water toward a small exit point you cut in one short wall.

Roll four wall strips 7 mm thick: two at 35 cm long by 3 cm tall (long sides) and two at 12 cm long by 3 cm tall (short sides). Allow all pieces to rest on the canvas for 20 minutes to stiffen slightly before joining. They should hold their shape when lifted but still feel cool and plastic.

Before attaching the short walls, cut a drainage slot into the base of one short wall strip. The slot should be 2 cm wide and 3 mm tall, positioned at the centre of the strip base. This aligns with the central channel in the base slab.
Use the
score-and-slip

method to attach each wall. Score the underside of each wall strip and the corresponding edge of the base slab. Apply slip to both scored surfaces. Press the long walls on first, standing them upright along the long edges of the base. Hold each wall firmly for 20 seconds and blend the interior join with a damp wooden rib.

Attach the short walls, scoring and slipping the ends of the short walls where they meet the already-attached long walls, as well as the base join. Press the joins firmly and blend all interior corners with the wooden rib, filling any gap with a small rolled rope of clay if needed.

Stand the tray upright on a flat surface. Press gently on the top edges of each wall with a finger to check they are level. If one wall sits higher than another, carefully trim the excess with the fettling knife at the top edge.

Run a damp sponge along all exterior joins to clean up any slip residue. Smooth the exterior corners by pressing the wooden rib diagonally along the join line. Check all four internal corners are fully filled with no voids.

Roll four small clay feet, each a flattened ball about 1.5 cm across and 8 mm tall. Score the base of each foot and the base slab in the four corners of the tray. Apply slip and press firmly. The feet lift the tray base off the windowsill so any drainage has clearance.
Drying
Cover loosely with plastic for the first 24 hours to reach
leather-hard
. Check all four corners at this stage and press any opening joins closed with a damp fingertip. Remove the cover and dry to
bone-dry

over three to five days. Dry on the flat work surface rather than lifting: the tray is vulnerable at the base-to-wall join until fully dry. A bone-dry tray is pale throughout and makes a faint hollow sound when tapped.
Finishing

Apply two coats of diluted PVA to all surfaces, inside and out, allowing each coat to dry before applying the next. The seal makes the surface wipe-clean and gives basic water resistance, but the tray is still not suitable for standing water. Paint before sealing if you want colour, using acrylic paint on the bone-dry clay.
Care

This tray is decorative and suitable for standing potted plants. It is not waterproof: do not allow water to pool inside it. After watering plants, empty any standing water from the tray promptly. Wipe the inside of the tray dry after use. Keep indoors, away from direct weather exposure.
Variations

Press a simple repeating leaf stamp along the outside of the long walls before assembling the tray. Stamp into the soft clay of each wall strip while it is still flat on the table, then allow to stiffen before joining. The flat-stamping step is much easier than stamping a curved or joined surface.
Scale down to a single-pot saucer: 12 cm square base with 2 cm walls and no drainage channel. These work as matching under-saucers for individual pots arranged across a windowsill.
Inscribe the herb names along the top edge of the long wall using a needle tool at leather-hard. Space the names evenly to align with where each pot will sit. Seal and paint before placing pots.
Troubleshooter

items.problem: Corners open up or crack during drying
items.cause: The clay was too dry when the walls were joined, preventing a strong bond, or the interior corners were not blended adequately
items.fix: At leather-hard, dampen the crack with a wet sponge, apply fresh slip, and press closed. Fill any gap with a clay rope pushed into the corner with a wooden rib

items.problem: Tray base bows upward in the centre
items.cause: The base slab dried faster on top than underneath, pulling upward as the top face shrank more
items.fix: At leather-hard, press the base flat with a board weighted with a few books overnight. If already bone-dry, sit the tray on a damp cloth briefly to soften the base, press flat, and re-dry

items.problem: Walls lean inward at the top
items.cause: The walls were not supported while drying and the still-soft clay relaxed inward
items.fix: Pack crumpled paper inside the tray at leather-hard to hold the walls upright while the clay finishes firming. Remove before the paper causes cracking

items.cause: The feet were added when the base slab was already too stiff for a strong score-and-slip bond
items.fix: Re-attach at leather-hard with generous slip and hold firmly for 30 seconds. If at bone-dry stage, glue with neat PVA and allow to cure for 24 hours before moving the tray
